To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“cyber-directed vaccination is an effective strategy for interrupting disease transmission when the disease is spread through short-range contacts, and that the optimal vaccination strategy depends on the disease’s transmission characteristics.”
targeted vaccination, when possible, can enhance the efficiency of disease control efforts, but that the most effective targets are not necessarily those with the highest number of cyber contacts.

‘cyber-directed targeted vaccination can enhance the effectiveness of vaccination campaigns against diseases transmitted by short-range modes of transmission, but not against diseases transmitted by full-range modes of transmission’.
In summary, our research is concerned with
optimizing vaccination strategies in the context of cyber-physical networks, which may be useful to inform the design of vaccination strategies in the event of future disease outbreaks.
the question of how to best identify and vaccinate individuals in a population to reduce disease transmission and clinical impact.
the development of a mathematical simulation framework that can be applied to optimize targeted vaccination across cyber-physical networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

cyber networks can be used to identify individuals who should be targeted for vaccination to minimize the spread of a disease with short-range transmission, but that the use of cyber networks to target vaccination for a disease with full-range transmission is not recommended, at least for the specific population we studied.

cyber-directed vaccination can be a useful tool for optimizing vaccination campaigns in the context of a disease spreading on a physical proximity network, but it cannot be a panacea for all diseases and transmission scenarios.
cyber-directed vaccination may be a promising strategy for targeted vaccination against some infectious diseases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that cyber communication networks can indeed be used to enhance vaccination campaigns against certain types of diseases.
the digital footprint of individuals is not a good proxy for their social network in terms of disease transmission.
the cyber network can be a useful proxy for the physical network in the context of short-range disease transmission, but not for full-range transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that

digital communication networks can be used to identify individuals with the potential to interrupt disease transmission in the real world, and thus can help to advance the goal to achieve targeted vaccination.
the digital communication networks of individuals may reflect their underlying physical interactions, and this information can be used to improve targeted vaccination strategies.
cyber networks can be used to enhance the efficiency of targeted vaccination campaigns, but only if the disease transmission process is sufficiently constrained by short-range interactions.
